item.title: Perfectly aperiodic asymmetric scalable metasurface based on the hat monotile
item.description: arXiv:2610.32467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurfaces are conventionally designed on periodic lattices, which renders their electromagnetic response spatially uniform and leaves the spatial arrangement itself unused as an information-bearing design resource. In this study, we propose and numerically validate a metasurface built on an aperiodic monotile: the recently discovered "hat" polykite, a single tile mathematically guaranteed to tile the plane only nonperiodically. The twelve distinguishable orientations of the hat serve as a natural design basis; each carries resonant elements tuned to one of twelve absorption frequencies between 4.600 and 4.914 GHz, transcribing the provable aperiodicity and mirror asymmetry of the geometry into the electromagnetic response. Gaussian-beam scanning over a compositionally unique 6 times 6 grid yields irregular, position-dependent electromagnetic signatures whose pairwise separations reach beyond 6 dB. In particular, coherence-guided selection of multiple frequencies increases the stable rank of the position-signature matrix from 1.0 to approximately 1.6 with three frequency components, whereas the accumulation of mutually similar electromagnetic features fails to add effective dimensions, demonstrating that properly selected multifrequency characteristics enhance the spatial distinguishability embedded in the surface. A shift-correlation analysis in which the cosine similarity never exceeds 0.5 confirms that the response inherits the absence of translational order from the tiling. Compatible with standard printed-circuit fabrication, the aperiodic metasurface design establishes a deterministic route toward position-identifiable electromagnetic environments for localization, chipless identification, and integrated sensing and communication.
item.dc:creator: Yuma Otsuka, Hiroki Wakatsuchi

item.title: The Extended Diode Equation
item.description: arXiv:2610.32090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For more than 75 years, the p-n junction current-voltage characteristic has been derived by treating majority carriers as an inert background and conflating the junction voltage with the applied bias. Here we show that the base electric field, generated by the coupling of excess majority and minority carriers, fundamentally alters the internal potential distribution. This self-consistent framework yields a closed-form extended diode equation that reproduces the high-injection roll-off without invoking an external series resistance, thereby eliminating an empirical patch that has persisted in the classical theory.
item.dc:creator: Jianhong Yang, Gonghao Sun, Tinglan Li

item.title: A Self-Consistent Two-Carrier Drift-Diffusion Framework for p-n Junctions: Extended Diode Equation, Power Dissipation, and Base Transit Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.32112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The classical theory of p-n junctions derives the current-voltage characteristic from minority-carrier diffusion alone: majority carriers are treated as an inert background, the quasi-neutral base as field-free, and the junction voltage as equal to the applied bias. These premises fail together under high bias and high-level injection, where the observed current roll-off is reproduced only by appending an empirical series resistance outside the junction physics. Here we develop a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion framework that introduces no assumption beyond the classical ones. Excess majority carriers are shown to be electrostatically forced transport participants: the ambipolar diffusion equation, closed by exact two-sided boundary conditions, yields a unified excess-carrier profile. The resulting base field separates into an ohmic and a Dember component, and all four current components follow in closed form, their sum being position independent. At device level the framework closes into an extended diode equation that contains the Shockley equation as its low-injection, long-base limit and reproduces the n=2 roll-off intrinsically. The junction voltage emerges as a self-limiting drop confined to the space-charge region and separated from the applied bias by exact base drops. Two device-level corrections are quantified: at high current, 75-90% of the dissipation migrates from the junction into the quasi-neutral base, and field-assisted acceleration shortens the base transit time by up to a factor of six. Three parameter-free predictions follow: a universal ideality-factor crossover that passes through 3/2 when the boundary excess equals the doping, a high-injection onset voltage that scales as 119 mV per decade of doping, and a geometry factor that survives into high injection.
item.dc:creator: Jianhong Yang, Tinglan Li, Gonghao Sun

item.title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
item.description: arXiv:2610.32154v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Measurements of photon-number-dependent time-of-arrival (TOA) distributions in wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors (SMSPDs) are presented. Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(\tau_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(\mu_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.
item.dc:creator: Hsin-Yeh Wu, Shu-Xiao Liu, Boris Tuchming, Xavier-Fran\c{c}ois Navick, Pu-Kai Wang, Yi-Ren Wu, Jia-Wern Chen, Marc Besan\c{c}on, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Glicenstein, Pisin Chen, Yu-Jung Lu, Stathes Paganis

item.title: From Hollow Waveguides to Mie Voids: Low-Index Light Confinement
item.description: arXiv:2610.32494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The confinement of light within optically thin media challenges the conventional view that optical localization requires high-index dielectric materials and total internal reflection. Over the past decades, a broad range of photonic phenomena has demonstrated that electromagnetic energy can also be guided and localized inside low-index regions or nanoscale void cavities. What first appears to be a curiosity is, in fact, highly relevant: The interaction between light and matter lies at the heart of much in optics and photonics. It enables sensing, nonlinear optical phenomena, and optical manipulation, yet it also inevitably introduces absorption, dissipation, and loss. Pushing localized, enhanced, or guided energy into a lower-index space thus offers entirely new possibilities for light-matter interaction and dispersion control. In this review, we discuss some of these counterintuitive structures, starting with light guidance within optically thin media, such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers or antiresonant reflecting optical waveguides. We then discuss the optics of bubbles, that is, low-index inclusions in a higher-index surrounding, and ultimately arrive at the so-called Mie void resonators, optical resonators that support localized electromagnetic modes confined within a region of lower refractive index. All these systems demonstrate that there are (resonant) optics beyond simple total internal reflection. Absence can itself become a functional photonic degree of freedom, opening opportunities across sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical matter.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Ludescher, Ivan Toftul, Harald Giessen, Yuri Kivshar, Mario Hentschel

item.title: Integrated elliptical III-V nanopillar arrays on silicon for dual photodetection and light emission
item.description: arXiv:2610.32744v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Next-generation on-chip photonic devices require compact, energy-efficient components integrating photodetection and light emission on silicon platforms. Achieving broadband photodetection combined with efficient emission in a single nanoscale device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate elliptical nanopillar arrays monolithically integrated as III-V-on-Si templates, exhibiting broadband photoresponse across visible to near-infrared wavelengths, dynamic neuron-like graded responses under modulated light, and pronounced electroluminescence at around 865 nm under forward bias. The nanostructured elliptical geometry approach enhances optical absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area significantly smaller than commercial detectors, enabling responsivities up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm in compact nanoarrays. This work advances the development of miniaturized active nanophotonic devices suitable for integrated sensing, emitting and communication circuits, and neuromorphic processing on silicon substrates.

item.title: Ginzburg-Landau Theory with Elastic Incompatibility Describes the Liquid-G-phase-Crystal State Diagram
item.description: arXiv:2610.32791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We derive a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory for the metastable heterogeneous G state reported in deeply undercooled metallic liquids. The central result is that type-II-like mixed-state physics can emerge structurally with the random internal stress field playing the role of the magnetic field. Frozen eigenstrain due to elastic incompatibility between ordered cores and the amorphous matrix generates incompatible stress, while the non-affine internal strain in the liquid-like matrix in between the ordered cores relaxes that stress over a finite screening length $\lambda_\sigma$ (analogous to the London length in the superconducting problem). Structural order heals over a distinct mechanically-dressed length $\xi_G$; their ratio $\kappa_G=\lambda_\sigma/\xi_G$ provides the structural counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter. Because the matrix is transiently rigid yet locally relaxational only over an intermediate time window, the same mechanism selects crystal for slow protocols, a heterogeneous G state at intermediate rates, and a homogeneous L-like glass under rapid arrest. Residual incompatibility frustrates coarsening, allowing finite ordered cores and screened, orientation-dependent core interactions. The resulting texture is an inverted Abrikosov analogue: structural order resides in the cores, whereas incompatible-stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory yields direct simulation and experimental tests through stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine-susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Zaccone, Konrad Samwer

item.title: A Compact Single-Beam Optically Pumped Magnetometer Based on Absorption Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.32795v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate a compact single-beam optically pumped magnetometer (OPM) employing a pure 87Rb microfabricated vapor cell with 500 Torr buffer gas. The residual magnetic field is actively minimized to below 400 pT through a combination of mu-metal magnetic shielding and internal compensation coils. We systematically characterize the OPM response as a function of laser detuning and optical intensity, and derive the magnetic-field sensitivity from the signal slope and noise amplitude spectral density. A best sensitivity of 11 fT/Hz^1/2 is achieved near the resonance transition at an optimal optical intensity, using a small cell volume of only 0.027 cm^3. Furthermore, a miniaturized OPM prototype was developed using a folded flexible printed circuit board (FPCB) to integrate the vapor cell, a compact heater, and magnetic-field coils into a cubic sensing head. Two coil configurations patterned directly on the FPCB were investigated. Under optimized operating conditions, the OPM prototype achieved a sensitivity of 66 fT/Hz^1/2. These results demonstrate that high-buffer-pressure single-beam OPMs can achieve excellent sensitivity, establishing a pathway toward compact and scalable arrays.
item.dc:creator: Jia-You Liou, Yi-Hsuan Chen, Hsiang-An Chuang, Chih-Hsuan Huang, Zong-Hsin Liu, I-Chiao Tsai, Kai-Hsin Peng, Yi-Hsin Chen

item.title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.32924v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Scaling of Laser Processing - Making Light Matter, edited by J. Bonse and A. F. Lasagni, 2026, Springer Nature Switzerland AG

item.title: Thermoelastic wave-based logic for mechanically cognitive materials
item.description: arXiv:2511.00647v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in metamaterials and fabrication techniques have revived interest in mechanical computing. Contrary to techniques relying on static deformations of buckling beams or origami-based lattices, the integration of wave scattering and mechanical memory presents a promising path toward efficient, low-latency elastoacoustic computing. This work introduces a novel class of multifunctional mechanical computing circuits that leverage the rich dynamics of phononic and locally resonant materials. These circuits incorporate memory-integrated components, realized here via metamaterial cells infused with shape memory alloys which recall stored elastic profiles and trigger specific actions upon thermal activation. A critical advantage of this realization is its synergistic interaction with incident vibroacoustic loads and the inherited high speed of waves, as opposed to recent adaptations of mechanically intelligent systems that employ innately slower mechanisms such as elastomeric shape changes and snap-through bistabilities. Through a proof-of-concept physical implementation, the efficacy and reconfigurability of the wave-based gates are demonstrated via output probes and measured wavefields. Furthermore, the modular design of the fundamental gates can be used as building blocks to construct complex combinational logic circuits, paving the way for sequential logic in wave-based analog computing systems.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Fort, Mohamed Mousa, Mostafa Nouh

item.title: QubiC 2.0: An Extensible Open-Source Qubit Control System Capable of Mid-Circuit Measurement and Feed-Forward
item.description: arXiv:2309.10333v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Researchers manipulate and measure quantum processing units via the classical electronics control system. We developed an open-source FPGA-based quantum bit control system called QubiC for superconducting qubits. After years of qubit calibration and testing experience on QubiC 1.0, we recognized the need for mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward capabilities to implement advanced quantum algorithms, and upgraded the system to QubiC 2.0 on an AMD ZCU216 RFSoC evaluation board with all these enriched features. The system uses portable FPGA gateware with a simplified processor to handle commands on-the-fly. For design simplicity and straightforward scaling, we adopted a multi-core distributed architecture, assigning one processor core per qubit. The pulses combine the unique pulse envelope and carrier information specified in a command. Each pulse envelope is pre-stored in the FPGA's block RAMs, ensuring speed and reusability throughout the quantum circuit, while pulse parameters including amplitude, phase, and frequency can be updated from pulse to pulse. The software stack is developed in Python, running on both the FPGA's ARM core and a host computer via XML-RPC. Quantum circuits can be described in a high-level language supporting both pulse-level and native-gate-level programming with high-level control flow constructs, and are compiled into binary commands loaded into the FPGA. With QubiC 2.0, we achieved multi-FPGA synchronization and low-latency data communication, and demonstrated feed-forward experiments on conditional circuits. The system also serves as a platform for artificial intelligence and machine learning driven quantum control, such as FPGA-based real-time quantum state discrimination. The enhanced QubiC system provides researchers with powerful tools to explore and implement advanced quantum algorithms and applications.
item.dc:creator: Yilun Xu, Gang Huang, Neelay Fruitwala, Neel R. Vora, Abhi D. Rajagopala, Akel Hashim, Larry Chen, Noah Goss, Kasra Nowrouzi, Ravi K. Naik, Christopher Spitzer, David I. Santiago, Irfan Siddiqi

item.title: Arbitrary-order exceptional points in a nanomechanical cavity
item.description: arXiv:2512.11679v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exceptional points (EPs), non-Hermitian spectral singularities, shape the evolution dynamics ranging from topological mode control to high-precision sensing. Higher-order EPs unlock enriched and sharpened spectral topology beyond the minimal second-order counterpart, thus expanding capabilities in those domains. However, the intrinsic topological fragility of higher-order EPs has long hindered their robust experimental realization. Here, we present a scalable architecture that implements arbitrary-order EPs via an optically mediated recurrent network comprising a single nanomechanical resonator and an ensemble of digital synthetic resonators. We experimentally validate this architecture's scalability for both linear and nonlinear mechanical EPs, demonstrating EPs up to the seventh order. Moreover, we reveal that the fundamental noise component, in contrast to some technical-noise contributions, shares the same system coupling channel and undergoes identical root-response amplification as the measured signal. The co-amplification mechanism sets the fundamental sensitivity limit near EPs of any order, as verified by direct signal-to-noise ratio measurements. Our work establishes a general platform for exploring higher-order EP-based phenomena while clarifying the fundamental boundary of non-Hermitian sensitivity enhancement. More broadly, it facilitates a connection between non-Hermitian physics and AI-inspired recurrent architectures across diverse physical systems.
item.dc:creator: Ning Wu, Kaiyu Cui, Ziming Chen, Chenxuan Wang, Xue Feng, Fang Liu, Wei Zhang, Hao Sun, Yongzhuo Li, Yidong Huang

item.title: Synchrotron-based Photonuclear Neutron Source for Energy, Medicine and Radiation Testing
item.description: arXiv:2602.09172v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neutron source availability is constrained by the declining number of research reactors and the challenging cost of spallation facilities, while compact accelerator-based sources remain limited to beam powers below 100~kW due to severe thermal loads from charged particle-target interactions. Here we demonstrate that synchrotron-driven photonuclear production overcomes this fundamental limitation through architectural decoupling: electrons circulating in a storage ring generate MeV-range synchrotron radiation that drives external neutron production targets, completely isolating targets from primary charged-particle power. This separation enables continuous-wave photon beam powers exceeding 200~kW per beamline while drastically reducing localized heating and reducing thermal shocks. Through systematic Monte Carlo optimization across three independent codes (OpenMC, MCNPX, FLUKA), we identify optimal target configurations delivering single-beamline neutron intensities of $3$--$13 \times 10^{14}$~n/s with inherent spectral tunability: low-Z targets (Be, D$_2$O) produce epithermal-to-thermal spectra for medical applications, while high-Z converters (W, U) generate fast neutrons for subcritical reactors. Multi-beamline architecture enables facility-scale outputs exceeding $6 \times 10^{16}$~n/s, being competitive with research reactors, while supporting simultaneous parallel
